laws.historical_context: Collection of 57 judicial decisions and court rulings in Commercial law from Lebanese courts including the Court of Cassation, Courts of Appeal, Constitutional Council, Council of State, and specialized tribunals. These decisions establish important legal precedents in Lebanese jurisprudence.

key_articles.text_english: The Lebanese Court of Cassation held that the criteria for determining whether arbitration is international in nature are economic, specifically whether the underlying dispute involves a cross-border flow of goods or funds, as defined by Article 809 NCPC. The Court further ruled that interest awarded by arbitral tribunals may exceed the value of legal interest as determined by Lebanese law and that such awards are not subject to review in annulment proceedings. Legal principles established: International arbitration is determined by economic criteria: cross-border flow of goods or funds; Arbitral interest awards may exceed the statutory legal interest rate; Interest awards by arbitral tribunals are not reviewable in annulment proceedings Articles cited: Article 809 NCPC, Article 767 COC

key_articles.text_english: The Lebanese Court of Cassation confirmed that the doctrine of competence-competence applies to international arbitration proceedings in Lebanon, meaning an arbitral tribunal has priority to rule on its own jurisdiction before courts intervene. The Court also extended the binding effect of an arbitration agreement to a non-signatory company by virtue of the economic unity existing between that company and the signatories, without requiring the non-signatory to have participated in the drafting or execution of the agreement, or even to have knowledge of it. Legal principles established: Competence-competence doctrine applies to international arbitration in Lebanon; Non-signatory bound by arbitration agreement through economic unity principle; Economic unity test does not require participation in drafting, execution, or knowledge of the agreement Articles cited: Article 785 NCPC, Articles 766, 763 NCPC

key_articles.text_english: The Lebanese Court of Cassation established the conflict-of-law rule for determining the law governing arbitration agreements. The Court held that proof of an arbitration agreement and its extension over time is governed either by the law applicable to the effects of the agreement or by the law of the place where the agreement was concluded, as codified in Article 139(1) of the NCPC. This confirms that Lebanese courts apply classic conflict-of-law rules regardless of the place of arbitration. Legal principles established: Governing law of arbitration agreement is either law of effects or law of place of conclusion; Classic conflict-of-law rules apply regardless of seat of arbitration Articles cited: Article 139(1) NCPC

key_articles.text_english: The Lebanese Court of Cassation ruled that judges may act as arbitrators without legal restrictions, finding no statutory prohibition on active judges serving as arbitrators in private disputes. This decision confirmed Lebanese law's permissive approach to arbitrator eligibility. Legal principles established: No restriction on judges serving as arbitrators under Lebanese law; Permissive approach to arbitrator eligibility

key_articles.text_english: The Lebanese Court of Cassation held that an arbitral award cannot be annulled on the ground of violation of public policy merely because the arbitrator misinterpreted the law. The annulment process is not an appeal on the merits; errors of legal interpretation do not by themselves constitute a public policy violation sufficient to invalidate an award. Legal principles established: Annulment is not appeal on merits; Legal misinterpretation by arbitrator does not constitute public policy violation; Narrow scope of review in annulment proceedings

Legal principles established: Annulment is not appeal on merits; Legal misinterpretation by arbitrator does not constitute public policy violation; Narrow scope of review in annulment proceedings

key_articles.text_english: The Lebanese Court of Cassation reaffirmed that proceedings to set aside an arbitral award do not constitute an appeal on the merits or legality of the award. Courts reviewing annulment applications are precluded from examining the correctness of the arbitrator's factual or legal determinations. This decision solidified the boundary between annulment and appellate review. Legal principles established: Set-aside proceedings are not merits review; Courts cannot examine factual or legal correctness of arbitral awards in annulment; Clear separation between annulment and appeal

This decision solidified the boundary between annulment and appellate review. Legal principles established: Set-aside proceedings are not merits review; Courts cannot examine factual or legal correctness of arbitral awards in annulment; Clear separation between annulment and appeal

key_articles.text_english: The Lebanese Court of Cassation ruled that the 1958 New York Convention on Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards applies in Lebanon only when its provisions are more favorable to the party seeking enforcement than the provisions of the Lebanese New Code of Civil Procedure. Under the NCPC's international public policy standard, the NCPC was deemed more favorable, limiting the automatic application of the New York Convention. Legal principles established: New York Convention applies only when more favorable than NCPC; More-favorable-right rule applies to enforce arbitral awards; NCPC public policy standard is narrower than Convention's Articles cited: Article VII(1) New York Convention, Article 814 NCPC

key_articles.text_english: The Lebanese Court of Cassation held that the disqualification or recusal of an arbitrator does not invalidate the underlying arbitration agreement. The agreement survives the removal of a particular arbitrator, and proceedings may continue with a replacement arbitrator. Legal principles established: Arbitration agreement survives recusal/disqualification of arbitrator; Recusal does not annul the arbitration agreement Articles cited: Article 770(3) NCPC
key_articles.subject: [CASE LAW] Lebanese Court of Cassation - Decision 29/2002 (2002-02-28)
key_articles.title: Arbitrator Recusal Does Not Annul Arbitration Agreement

Legal principles established: Arbitration agreement survives recusal/disqualification of arbitrator; Recusal does not annul the arbitration agreement Articles cited: Article 770(3) NCPC

key_articles.text_english: The Lebanese Court of Cassation ruled that when an arbitrator is disqualified, his mandate is revoked retroactively, and any awards rendered by that arbitrator in the proceedings are annulled as a consequence. This is the converse of Decision 29/2002, which protected the agreement itself, but here the Court addressed the effect on awards already issued. Legal principles established: Arbitrator disqualification revokes mandate retroactively; Awards rendered by disqualified arbitrator are annulled

Legal principles established: Arbitrator disqualification revokes mandate retroactively; Awards rendered by disqualified arbitrator are annulled

key_articles.text_english: The Lebanese Court of Cassation held that Lebanese courts cannot raise the lack of arbitral jurisdiction on their own motion (ex officio). The existence of an arbitration clause is not a matter of public policy requiring courts to intervene spontaneously; parties must affirmatively invoke the arbitration agreement. If a party fails to raise the objection in a timely manner, it is deemed waived. Legal principles established: Arbitral jurisdiction is not a public policy issue courts must raise ex officio; Parties must affirmatively invoke arbitration agreements; Waiver of jurisdictional objection if not raised timely

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of Appeal affirmed that an arbitration agreement is legally independent and separable from the underlying contract in which it is contained. This means the invalidity, termination, or rescission of the main contract does not automatically render the arbitration clause null and void. The Court also held that parties may appoint a legal entity (as opposed to an individual) to serve in the role of appointing arbitrators. Legal principles established: Arbitration agreement is independent and separable from the main contract; Invalidity of main contract does not affect validity of arbitration clause; Legal entities may be appointed as arbitrator-appointing authorities

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of Appeal confirmed the separability doctrine by ruling that the invalidity of the main contract does not entail the invalidity of the arbitration agreement it contains. This is a landmark restatement of the separability principle in Lebanese arbitration law, ensuring parties cannot avoid arbitration by challenging the underlying contract. Legal principles established: Invalidity of main contract does not invalidate arbitration clause (separability); Parties cannot avoid arbitration by challenging the main contract

key_articles.title: Separability Doctrine - Invalidity of Main Contract

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of Appeal held that Lebanese courts generally refrain from excluding a matter from arbitration solely on the basis that it involves a question of public policy. The Court rejected an expansive interpretation of Article 1037 of the Code of Obligations and Contracts as a bar to arbitration, affirming that arbitration can resolve most commercial disputes even those touching on regulatory or public interest considerations. Legal principles established: Public policy alone does not render a dispute non-arbitrable; Narrow interpretation of non-arbitrability exceptions Articles cited: Articles 762, 765 NCPC, Article 1037 COC

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of First Instance ruled that Article 5 of Decree-Law 34/67, which grants Lebanese courts jurisdiction over commercial agency disputes, confers exclusive jurisdiction over other state courts (foreign courts) but not over arbitral tribunals. Therefore, disputes arising from commercial representation agreements are arbitrable and may be resolved by arbitration, reversing prior approaches that treated such disputes as non-arbitrable. Legal principles established: Article 5 of DL 34/67 grants exclusive jurisdiction over other state courts, not arbitral tribunals; Commercial agency disputes are arbitrable; Relevant to anti-suit injunctions in commercial representation contexts Articles cited: Article 5 of Decree-Law 34/67

key_articles.text_english: The 9th Chamber of the Beirut Court of Appeal ruled that an arbitration clause in a commercial agency agreement is null and void under Article 5 of Decree-Law No. 34/67, which was interpreted to render all such disputes non-arbitrable. The Court held that the 1958 New York Convention only applies to disputes capable of arbitration under the lex fori, and since Lebanese law excluded commercial agency disputes under Article 5, the clause was invalid and the court retained jurisdiction. Legal principles established: Pre-dispute arbitration clause in agency agreement is null and void; Article 5 of DL 34/67 rendered agency disputes non-arbitrable (pre-2015 interpretation); New York Convention limited to disputes arbitrable under the law of the seised court Articles cited: Article 5 of Decree-Law 34 of August 5, 1967, 1958 New York Convention

Legal principles established: Pre-dispute arbitration clause in agency agreement is null and void; Article 5 of DL 34/67 rendered agency disputes non-arbitrable (pre-2015 interpretation); New York Convention limited to disputes arbitrable under the law of the seised court Articles cited: Article 5 of Decree-Law 34 of August 5, 1967, 1958 New York Convention

key_articles.text_english: The Lebanese Court of Cassation drew a critical distinction between an arbitration clause (signed before or during agency agreement) and an arbitration agreement (concluded after the dispute arises). It ruled that while a pre-dispute arbitration clause in a commercial agency contract is void under Article 5 of DL 34/67, a post-dispute arbitration agreement is valid. After the dispute arises, the Lebanese representative is no longer in a subordinate position and can freely waive the statutory protections of Article 5. Legal principles established: Post-dispute arbitration agreement in agency context is valid; Pre-dispute arbitration clause in agency agreement remains void; After dispute arises, representative is free to agree to arbitration; Protective purpose of Article 5 DL 34/67 no longer applies once dispute has arisen Articles cited: Article 5 of Decree-Law 34 of August 5, 1967

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of First Instance held that a company's insolvency or entry into liquidation does not render its arbitration agreements null and void. The liquidator is bound to enforce outstanding arbitration agreements. The Court also confirmed that the absence of an express provision specifying the number of arbitrators in an arbitration agreement does not invalidate that agreement. Legal principles established: Insolvency does not nullify pre-existing arbitration agreements; Liquidator must enforce arbitration agreements; Absence of express arbitrator number does not nullify agreement

Legal principles established: Insolvency does not nullify pre-existing arbitration agreements; Liquidator must enforce arbitration agreements; Absence of express arbitrator number does not nullify agreement

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of First Instance held that a party who did not sign an arbitration agreement may nonetheless be bound by it if that party participated in the negotiation or implementation of the underlying agreement. This extends the reach of arbitration clauses to parties who are functionally part of the contractual relationship even if not formal signatories. Legal principles established: Participation in negotiation or implementation of agreement can bind non-signatories; Non-signatory test: substantive participation, not just formal signature

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of Appeal confirmed that arbitral proceedings and awards are confidential by nature, unlike public court judgments. The private nature of arbitration, combined with Article 553 NCPC and Article 788 NCPC, ensures that deliberations are secret and awards are not subject to the general principle of public access to justice that applies in state court proceedings. Legal principles established: Arbitral proceedings and awards are confidential; Confidentiality distinguishes arbitration from public court process; Deliberations of arbitral tribunals are secret Articles cited: Article 553 NCPC, Article 788 NCPC

The review is strictly limited to jurisdictional issues and procedural public policy, not the substantive correctness of the arbitral decision. Legal principles established: No review of award grounds or legal compliance in set-aside proceedings; Set-aside limited to jurisdictional and procedural public policy issues

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of Appeal ruled that the domestic NCPC procedural rules for challenging arbitrators apply to international ad hoc arbitration proceedings seated in Lebanon. The Court rejected arguments that international arbitration should follow different challenge procedures, applying the same standards for impartiality and independence that apply in domestic cases. Legal principles established: Domestic NCPC challenge rules apply to international ad hoc arbitration in Lebanon; Same impartiality and independence standards apply regardless of international or domestic nature Articles cited: Articles 770, 787(2) NCPC

Legal principles established: Domestic NCPC challenge rules apply to international ad hoc arbitration in Lebanon; Same impartiality and independence standards apply regardless of international or domestic nature Articles cited: Articles 770, 787(2) NCPC

key_articles.text_english: The Lebanese Court of Cassation established early precedent that in commercial matters, parties are free to determine the interest rate applicable to their contractual relationship by agreement. There is no legal cap on interest rates in commercial transactions, and courts cannot modify interest rates agreed upon by sophisticated commercial parties. Legal principles established: Commercial parties may freely determine interest rates in their agreements; No statutory cap on interest rates in commercial matters

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of Appeal (First Chamber) extended the binding effect of an arbitration clause to a third party based on the concept of 'economic unity' or a single economic operation ('opération économique unique'). Even though the third party had not signed the main agreement containing the arbitration clause, the economic unity linking the chain of contracts rendered the arbitration clause applicable to it. Legal principles established: Arbitration clause may extend to third party via economic unity principle; Single economic operation can bind non-signatories to arbitration

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of Appeal held that courts do not have concurrent jurisdiction with arbitral tribunals for interim payment orders that would involve examining the merits of the dispute. Courts may assist with enforcement-type interim measures pre-tribunal formation, but provisional payment requests that require substantive assessment fall within the exclusive competence of the arbitral tribunal. Legal principles established: No concurrent court jurisdiction for interim payments requiring merits analysis; Courts may assist with enforcement-type interim measures pre-tribunal; Substantive interim relief falls within arbitral tribunal's domain

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of Appeal granted enforcement (exequatur) to an arbitral award issued by an even-numbered tribunal in an international arbitration. Under the domestic NCPC rules for domestic arbitration, odd-numbered tribunals are standard, but the Court confirmed that for international arbitration, even-numbered panels are permissible and their awards can be enforced. Legal principles established: Even-numbered arbitral tribunals are permissible in international arbitration; Awards from even-numbered tribunals are enforceable in Lebanon Articles cited: Article 810 NCPC

Legal principles established: Even-numbered arbitral tribunals are permissible in international arbitration; Awards from even-numbered tribunals are enforceable in Lebanon Articles cited: Article 810 NCPC

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of Appeal held that a state-owned or state-related entity (including an Iraqi bank with state interference) that conducts commercial operations subject to private law cannot claim immunity from execution when a judgment or arbitral award is entered against it. The court distinguished between governmental functions (which may attract immunity) and commercial activities (which do not). Legal principles established: State-related entities conducting commercial operations cannot claim immunity from execution; Commercial activities are subject to private law enforcement; State interference does not transform commercial entity into immune state actor Articles cited: Article 860 LCCP

No merits review of the award's factual findings, legal analysis, or procedural correctness may take place in exequatur proceedings. This decision reinforced the minimal-intervention principle in the enforcement of international arbitral awards. Legal principles established: Exequatur review limited to manifest international public policy violation; No merits review permitted in exequatur of international arbitral awards; Strong pro-enforcement policy in Lebanon for international arbitral awards

key_articles.text_english: The Court of Appeal of Mount Lebanon confirmed that a decision by an arbitral tribunal on its own jurisdiction cannot be challenged or appealed before a final award is issued. Following the Court of Cassation's Decision 13/2007, this ruling confirmed that Article 615 NCPC (which lists challengeable interlocutory decisions in court proceedings) must be transposed to arbitration, and jurisdictional decisions are not on that list. Challenges to jurisdiction must wait until the final award is rendered. Legal principles established: Arbitral tribunal's jurisdiction decision not appealable before final award; Article 615 NCPC applied by analogy to arbitration proceedings; Jurisdictional challenges must be raised at annulment/enforcement stage Articles cited: Articles 615, 804 NCPC

Each party with distinct interests has the right to participate in the constitution of the arbitral tribunal. Legal principles established: Equality principle in arbitrator appointment is public policy; Separate respondents with distinct interests cannot be compelled to share one arbitrator; Multiparty arbitration must respect equality in tribunal constitution

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of Appeal reaffirmed that annulment proceedings do not permit a review of the grounds, reasoning, or legal compliance of an arbitral award. The court's role in annulment is strictly supervisory and procedural, not substantive. Any error in law or fact by the arbitral tribunal does not constitute a ground for annulment unless it rises to the level of a violation of public policy or breach of due process. Legal principles established: Annulment courts cannot review grounds or law compliance of arbitral awards; Strict separation between annulment and appellate review; Legal/factual errors by arbitrators are not annulment grounds unless public policy breached

Courts should apply severance principles to preserve the valid components of the arbitration agreement, treating the invalid provision as severable. This upholds the general pro-arbitration presumption in Lebanese law. Legal principles established: Severability applies to arbitration agreements - invalid term does not void entire agreement; Pro-arbitration presumption favors preserving valid components; Courts sever invalid provisions rather than nullifying entire arbitration agreement

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of Appeal established that the criteria for determining whether arbitration is international in nature are economic rather than formal or legal. An arbitration is international if the underlying transaction involves cross-border flows of goods, services, or funds. This economic test, later confirmed by the Court of Cassation in Decision 98/2006, remains the controlling standard for classifying arbitrations under the NCPC's different domestic and international arbitration regimes. Legal principles established: Internationality of arbitration determined by economic criteria; Cross-border flow of goods, services, or funds establishes international character; Formal or national/legal criteria not determinative of international arbitration status Articles cited: Article 809 NCPC

key_articles.text_english: The Special Tribunal for Lebanon Trial Chamber issued its long-awaited judgment in the assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafiq Hariri and 21 others on 14 February 2005. The Trial Chamber, comprising Judge David Re (Presiding), Judge Janet Nosworthy, and Lebanese Judge Micheline Braidy, found Salim Jamil Ayyash guilty beyond reasonable doubt on all five counts: conspiracy to commit a terrorist act, committing a terrorist act by explosive device, and three counts of intentional homicide/attempted homicide. Ayyash was convicted in absentia, primarily on circumstantial evidence from mobile phone records linking him to surveillance and coordination. The three co-accused (Hassan Habib Merhi, Hussein Hassan Oneissi, and Assad Hassan Sabra) were acquitted. On 11 December 2020, the sentencing chamber imposed five concurrent life sentences on Ayyash. key_articles.text_english: In a landmark pre-trial decision, the STL Appeals Chamber (presided by Judge Antonio Cassese) issued groundbreaking rulings on the definition of terrorism under customary international law and modes of criminal participation. The Chamber held that terrorism requires: (i) commission of a criminal act or threat thereof; (ii) intent to spread fear or coerce an authority; and (iii) a transnational element. The ruling established that attacks using ordinary firearms can constitute terrorism if they meet these criteria, contrary to prior Lebanese case law. The Chamber adopted Joint Criminal Enterprise I and II as modes of liability for terrorism but rejected JCE III (recklessness) and ICC 'perpetration by means' as incompatible with terrorism's specific intent requirement, preferring aiding and abetting instead. key_articles.text_english: In a landmark administrative ruling, the Lebanese State Shura Council (Lebanon's highest administrative court) found that the Lebanese State failed in its obligations under the 2017 Anti-Torture Law to prohibit, prevent, and adequately investigate torture allegations made by actor Ziad Itani. Itani had been arrested on fabricated spying charges in November 2017, subjected to torture and solitary confinement, denied access to a lawyer, and acquitted by military court in March 2018. The Council found the State failed to protect the presumption of innocence, failed to prosecute torturers (who were instead promoted), and failed to conduct required investigations. It ordered the State to pay Itani 480 million Lebanese Liras (approximately USD 5,360) in reparations. This was the first judicial application of Lebanon's 2017 anti-torture law by the administrative judiciary. Legal principles established: State has affirmative duty to prohibit, prevent, and investigate torture; Failure to prosecute perpetrators of torture constitutes state liability; Presumption of innocence must be protected by authorities, not undermined by press disclosures; Anti-torture law creates enforceable administrative duties on the State; State accountability for systemic torture impunity Articles cited: Anti-Torture Law No. 65/2017 (Lebanon, October 2017), Lebanese Constitution

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Court of First Instance dismissed a bankruptcy petition filed by a depositor against a Lebanese bank for failure to pay deposits. The Court ruled that standard bank insolvency provisions do not apply when the bank's cessation of payment results from a systemic 'comprehensive crisis' rather than an individual bank failure. Since the Banque du Liban (BDL) had failed to pay its obligations to commercial banks (despite the State's responsibility under Article 113 of the Monetary and Credit Law), the Court found that 'what applies to one bank applies to all banks.' The decision was criticized by The Legal Agenda for shielding banks from accountability and ignoring individual bank responsibility for investing deposits imprudently. Legal principles established: Standard bankruptcy provisions inapplicable during systemic banking crisis; Collective/regulatory crisis distinguishes from individual insolvency scenario; BDL failure to repay creates force majeure-type defense for commercial banks; State responsible under Article 113 Monetary and Credit Law for BDL losses Articles cited: Article 113 Monetary and Credit Law, Lebanese Commercial Code (bankruptcy provisions)

key_articles.text_english: The Beirut Urgent Matters Judge issued the most notable early ruling in Lebanon's banking crisis, ordering Byblos Bank SAL to transfer USD 1,138,085 to the plaintiff depositor's account at HSBC Bank in Dubai, subject to a coercive fine of 10 million Lebanese Pounds per day of delay. Byblos Bank had refused, citing BDL Circular of 4/12/2019 and the Association of Banks' circular imposing de facto capital controls. This decision was significant as one of the first pro-depositor rulings against Lebanese banks, though higher courts later adopted more restrictive approaches. Legal principles established: Bank's contractual obligation to execute international transfers is enforceable by specific performance; BDL circulars imposing capital controls do not eliminate contractual obligation to depositors; Coercive fines (astreinte) available to enforce banking transfer obligations Articles cited: Lebanese Code of Civil Procedure (urgent matters jurisdiction), Monetary and Credit Law

key_articles.text_english: The Lebanese Court of Cassation issued a series of rulings reversing the earlier pro-depositor trend in summary proceedings (référés). While lower judges had ordered banks to transfer funds overseas at depositors' requests, the Court of Cassation adopted a more restrictive stance, limiting the scope of relief available to depositors in urgent/summary proceedings. This shift forced depositors to seek alternative remedies including ex parte provisional seizures or merits-based actions. Legal principles established: Summary proceedings have limited scope for ordering international fund transfers; Depositors must pursue merits actions rather than urgent proceedings for banking transfers; Court of Cassation set limits on lower courts' expansive pro-depositor interpretations Articles cited: Lebanese Code of Civil Procedure (summary proceedings provisions)

key_articles.text_english: In a groundbreaking ruling, the Beirut Civil Court recognized the validity of a civil marriage conducted remotely via Zoom between two Lebanese citizens, officiated by a civil registrar in the State of Utah, USA. This is the first Lebanese court decision to validate a civil marriage contracted without religious oversight, conducted remotely, and outside Lebanese territory. The Court applied U.S. law and private international law principles, including freedom of conscience and the right to marry. The ruling may open space for civil marriage in Lebanon and is relevant to ongoing parliamentary debates about a unified personal status code. Legal principles established: Civil marriage conducted remotely by foreign civil registrar may be recognized in Lebanon; Private international law principles allow recognition of foreign civil marriages; Freedom of conscience and right to marry support recognition of civil unions; Lebanese courts may apply foreign law to validate marriages outside religious framework Articles cited: U.S. Utah State Marriage Law, Lebanese Private International Law principles, Lebanese Constitution Article 9 (freedom of religion/conscience)

key_articles.text_english: The Lebanese Court of Cassation interpreted the 2002 Law on Child Protection to grant civil courts jurisdiction not only over procedural matters in child custody disputes, but also over substantive issues where religious court judgments conflict with child welfare and public order principles. The Court ruled that civil courts may refuse to give civil recognition and force of law to any religious personal status judgment that contravenes the basic component of public order: child welfare and protection. This was the first time the Court of Cassation granted civil courts substantive (not merely procedural) jurisdiction over personal status matters. Legal principles established: Civil courts may refuse recognition of religious court judgments violating child welfare; Child welfare is a component of public order overriding religious personal status law; 2002 Child Protection Law grants civil courts substantive as well as procedural jurisdiction Articles cited: Lebanese Law on Child Protection (2002)
